description: Space lovers + code + tea ☕ Here to build something cool!
summary:
We developed AstraMed, an offline-first health self-assessment app for astronauts on long missions. On the way to the Moon or Mars, help from Earth arrives late: a signal takes about 1.3 seconds one way from the Moon and about 12.5 minutes from Mars at 140 million miles, and there are periods with no link at all. NASA's Human Research Program names five hazards of spaceflight - radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. Far from Earth, the crew's own daily check becomes the first line of care.
Once a day, an astronaut logs simple readings in under a minute: resting and standing heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, exercise, vision changes and symptoms, plus the mission radiation dose. AstraMed turns them into a 3D holographic body with seven zones, each linked to NASA HRP risks: heart and circulation; bones and muscles; eyes and head; immune system and skin; mind, sleep and crew; metabolism and nutrition; whole body and radiation. Every zone shows Normal, Attention or Critical, and every alert answers "Why am I seeing this?" in plain language.
The app tells the astronaut what to do now, when to involve the crew, and when to contact the flight surgeon. It builds a report for the surgeon that waits in a queue until Earth is reachable. All data stays on the crew member's device: no account, no server, no connection needed. AstraMed is decision support, not a diagnosis.
details:
AstraMed is a visual health file that an astronaut can read and act on without Earth. When a judge opens the link, a fictional crew member is already on mission day 60 of a Mars transit, with 60 days of demo history, so every feature can be seen in seconds.

Daily check-in (under 60 seconds). Large controls, steppers and icon choices for mood, sleep quality and team climate. Numeric fields have units and validation. A mission-day routine reminds the crew what to measure and when.

One clear overview. A 3D holographic body with seven zones and enunciator-style lamp grid. Hover or tap a zone to highlight it; click it and camera moves to the zone and open its card.

Zone cards that teach. Each indicator has 4 short blocks: How to measure? Why it matters? How spaceflight affects it? What to do? plus a chart (7 days/ 30 days/ all) with the personal baseline band, the threshold lines and a week-ago-vs-now comparison.

Alerts in three tiers. Attention is quiet. Critical must be acknowledged through a Master Caution control. The two most important alerts show first, the rest sit behind "Show all". Every alert explains why it fired.

Who to call. Actions are tiered: handle it yourself, tell the crew, or contact the flight surgeon.

Report for the flight surgeon. A 7 and 30-day summary with flagged values, symptoms and actions taken, as PDF and JSON. It is queued and sent when the simulated Earth link comes back.

Two languages and two themes. English and Russian for the app and the Guide; dark and light theme. The 3D body always stays in a dark viewing so the hologram stays readable.

Accessibility. Status is never color alone. Full keyboard operation, visible focus, WCAG AA contrast, and a static 2D body when WebGL is missing or the user prefers reduced motion. Works from a 375px phone to a laptop.

How does it work?

Every step runs on the crew member's device:

Daily check-in → local store (browser storage) → rules engine → zone status and alerts → report queue → Earth link (simulated).

The rules engine is data-driven: all limits live in one file (data/thresholds.json), each with its source and a verbatim quote. For each reading it applies four kinds of rules:

1 Reference range — published clinical ranges (for example American Heart Association blood-pressure categories, MedlinePlus temperature and SpO2 ranges, American Diabetes Association glucose cut-offs, CDC sleep guidance).

2 Personal pre-flight baseline — a value can be "normal" for the population but unusual for this astronaut; the app compares with their own baseline.

3 Seven-day trend — a slow drift in one direction raises Attention even while values are still in range (example in the demo: systolic pressure rising about 7 mmHg over 7 days).

4 Combined risk — poor sleep plus low mood plus team tension together raise a behavioural warning that no single value would trigger.

Radiation: the whole-body zone weighs the mission dose against NASA's career limit of 600 mSv (NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev. C, [V1 4030]). Daily dose rates per environment come from published measurements: ISS 0.731 mSv/day and Moon surface 1.369 mSv/day (Zhang et al., Science Advances 2020), Mars transit 1.8 mSv/day and Mars surface 0.67 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD, Hassler et al., Science 2014).

Honesty about limits: any rule without a published limit is stamped "team heuristic" on screen, and anything we could not verify is labelled "placeholder — not verified". Nothing is hidden behind a score.

Offline-first: all libraries, fonts and the 3D model are bundled with the app; a service worker caches every file, so after the first visit the app works with no network at all — which is the normal situation in deep space. Data never leaves the device unless the crew member exports it.

Tested: 13 automated tests cover the rules engine (ranges, baseline, trend, combined rule, environments). Lighthouse accessibility audit: 100 for the Guide, 97 for the app.

How AstraMed answers NASA's questions from the challenge

Challenge question

AstraMed's answer

Which measurements can be performed in space?

Low-equipment readings that fit a spacecraft: heart rate (resting and standing), blood pressure with a cuff, SpO2 with a finger oximeter, body temperature, fasting glucose with a meter, sleep hours (a wrist actigraph can fill this in), mood and team climate scales, exercise log, vision changes and a symptom checklist, and the radiation dose from the onboard dosimeter.

Why is each exam needed?

Each indicator belongs to a zone that is linked to a NASA HRP risk; the "Why it matters" block explains it in one or two lines.

How do spaceflight hazards affect each indicator?

Every card has a "How spaceflight affects it" block — for example fluid shift and blood pressure, eye and brain changes (SANS) with NASA-studied countermeasures such as thigh cuffs and a daily B-vitamin supplement, isolation and mood.

When should the crew or ground flight surgeons be involved?

When a value reaches Critical, when an Attention trend persists, or when several risk factors combine. The app then shows "contact the flight surgeon" and prepares the report.

What actions prevent a critical condition?

Each card has a tiered action plan: rest, exercise, sleep, nutrition and hydration, evidence-based countermeasures, then crew and surgeon escalation.

What benefits does it have?

• Autonomy: the crew can judge their own health during long delays and blackouts.

• Early warning: personal baseline and trend rules catch slow changes before they become critical.

• Trust: every status explains itself and shows where its limit comes from — no black box, no invented numbers.

• Privacy: health data stays on the device.

• Low workload: one check-in a day, one glance at the body, one clear status.

• Benefit on Earth: the same offline self-check can serve people far from a doctor — polar and remote stations, ships, mountain villages; space-health research also helps with bone loss, balance, heart and metabolic conditions.

What do we hope to achieve?

• Validate every threshold and the "team heuristic" rules with flight surgeons and physicians.

• Connect wearable sensors (heart rate, SpO2, actigraphy, dosimeter) so fewer values need typing, and add image input (camera photos of devices or skin) — not built yet.

• Real two-way sync with mission control whenever the link is available.

• Test with analog-mission crews before any real use.

Limitations (stated honestly): AstraMed is decision support, not a diagnosis. The demo astronaut and data are fictional. Reference ranges are Earth-based clinical values. It has not been tested with a real crew. The Russian translation has not yet been proofread by a native speaker with medical knowledge; the PDF report is in English only.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

• Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (ES modules), JSON. No build step, no backend.

• Libraries (bundled, open licences): three.js 0.187.0 (3D body, bloom), GSAP 3.15.1 (motion), Apache ECharts 6.1.0 (charts), jsPDF 4.2.1 (report).

• Web platform: Service Worker and Web App Manifest (installable, offline PWA), localStorage, Web Audio API (all sound is synthesised in code; off by default).

• 3D model: "Animated Human" by Quaternius (CC0). Fonts: Archivo and Literata (SIL Open Font License).

• Testing: Node.js test script for the rules engine, headless Chrome screenshots, Lighthouse.

• Hosting: GitHub Pages. Hardware: our laptops; the app runs on any modern browser, phone to desktop.

LINK GITHUB ------- https://github.com/osiyasadulloeva3-arch/astramed

• AI: Claude Code (see the AI section).

Our signature: made by team Lyra in Dushanbe, Tajikistan. The seven zones echo the seven stars of our flag as an abstract arc (not the flag or emblem); an optional sound motif is inspired by Tajik Shashmaqam.
